title: CI in the Era of AI: From Unit Tests to Stochastic Evals — Nathan Sobo, Zed
talk_summary: Zed's co-founder describes how they test LLM-driven agentic editing by starting with broad stochastic evals, then zooming into focused stochastic unit tests, then driving failures down to deterministic tests. The key mechanism is running the same eval 100-200 times and asserting a pass threshold, then converting each discovered failure mode into a cheap deterministic regression test.

takeaways.technique: Zoom-in eval ladder (eval -> stochastic unit test -> deterministic test)
takeaways.what_they_do: Start with a broad end-to-end eval, and whenever it fails, write a narrower stochastic test that exercises just that failure mode against the model, then convert the root cause into a fully deterministic test that runs in the normal suite.
takeaways.evidence_quote: starting with the zoomed out eval then zooming into a sort of stochastic unit test ... and then finally that driving that even further to an actual good oldfashioned test

takeaways.what_they_do: Run an eval N times in the normal test suite and fail the build unless a pass-rate watermark is met, rather than requiring a single deterministic pass.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we want 100% of these 200 examples to pass or this test should like literally fail the build
takeaways.numbers: 200 iterations, 100% pass threshold for that eval

takeaways.technique: Bounded non-determinism via randomized input chunking
takeaways.what_they_do: Randomly chunk streamed model output at arbitrary boundaries and run 100 iterations to prove the parser handles any chunking, turning a flaky streaming problem into a deterministic test.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we're going to run a 100 iterations of this very simple parsing test where we're randomly chunking up the input into arbitrary boundaries

takeaways.technique: Fuzzy matching + indent normalization for edit tool calls
takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of failing when the model emits slightly wrong old-text (indentation flattened, minor mismatch), use dynamic-programming approximate matching and renormalize indentation deltas so edits still apply.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Being able to do this dynamic programming that gets us an approximate match really saved a lot of the tool calling failures for us

takeaways.technique: Prompt fix then robustness fallback for malformed model output
takeaways.what_they_do: When the model mismatched XML tags ~40% of the time, a prompt instruction ('always close all tags properly') cut it to ~5%; the remaining 5% is handled by tolerant parsing rather than more prompting.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we were able to move that by saying always close all tags properly to like 95%

takeaways.technique: No external eval framework; reuse existing test infra
takeaways.what_they_do: They run evals inside the ordinary test suite using the same infrastructure as normal tests, avoiding special eval tooling.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we so far haven't needed to use like special external tools um or eval frameworks ... It's just in our test suite
